awd_titl_txt: Conference: Stem Cells, Cell Therapies, and Bioengineering in Lung Biology and Diseases
awd_abstract_narration:
The 2025 conference on Stem Cells, Cell Therapies, and Bioengineering in Lung Biology and Diseases at the University of Vermont in Burlington, 7-10 July 2025, will mark the 20th anniversary of this important biennial meeting. Over the past two decades, this conference has provided a platform for advancing research and collaboration in lung biology. This meeting stimulates discussion and debate by international leaders, new and emerging investigators, and trainees in the field. Meeting participants will also develop and publish guidelines for investigators and funding agencies on basic and translational research in stem cells, lung biology, and bioengineering. Junior investigators and trainees will involved in conference organization, oral presentations, chairing activities, discussions, and poster sessions. In 2025 the High School Science, Technology, Engineering, and Math (STEM) Experience will be expanded. This program will cultivate the next generation of scientists by providing an opportunity for high school students to engage with scientists from around the world and learn about state-of-the-art scientific techniques.

The repair and regeneration of diseased lungs using stem cells or bioengineered tissues represent transformative therapeutic strategies for a range of lung diseases and critical illnesses. Advances in preclinical models have demonstrated the potential for stem cell-based approaches to modulate immune responses and facilitate tissue repair following lung injury. Additionally, bioengineering research using artificial and acellular matrices as scaffolds for three-dimensional lung and airway regeneration has made strides, including promising transplantation attempts in large animal models. These efforts are complemented by a growing understanding of how endogenous lung stem and progenitor cells differentiate and contribute to repair and remodeling during lung development and after injury. In addition to attracting leading figures in lung biology and disease, the conference regularly features renowned stem cell experts from other disciplines, facilitating cross-pollination of ideas and innovation. For the 2025 conference, scientific symposia have been chosen to reflect the most cutting-edge advances in the field and will include sessions focusing on the integration of omics with function, matrix-cell dynamics, and immune cell contributions to repair and regeneration. Sessions will explore how inflammatory and mechanical cues influence stem cell regulation and highlight technological breakthroughs in bioengineering, such as precision-cut lung slices, hydrogels, and biomechanical modulation of lung function. These cutting edge basic and translational science studies are rapidly enhancing fundamental understanding of lung repair and regeneration, and the planned conference will continue to help shape further progress.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The 2025 Stem Cells, Cell Therapies, and Bioengineering in Lung Biology and Diseases Conference brought together scientists, physicians, engineers, trainees, and industry leaders from around the world to accelerate the development of new treatments for lung diseases. Held at the University of Vermont, the conference celebrated its 20th anniversary as the only international meeting dedicated exclusively to applying stem cell science, regenerative medicine, and bioengineering to improve lung health.

The conference welcomed 164 participants from 15 countries, 5 continents, and 20 U.S. states, creating a unique forum for sharing discoveries and building collaborations. Participants presented the latest advances in understanding how lungs develop, repair themselves after injury, and respond to disease. Researchers also highlighted new technologies, including stem cell-derived lung organoids, engineered tissues, precision-cut lung slices, advanced imaging, biomaterials, and computational approaches that are improving the study of diseases such as pulmonary fibrosis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), and other chronic lung conditions. These advances are helping move promising laboratory discoveries closer to future therapies for patients.

A major outcome of the conference was the development of new collaborations across disciplines. By bringing together experts in biology, engineering, medicine, and computational science, the meeting encouraged innovative approaches that no single field could achieve alone. Discussions throughout the conference identified critical scientific challenges and opportunities that will guide future research priorities. These recommendations are being compiled into a community white paper that will be shared publicly and with funding agencies to help shape future investments in lung regenerative medicine.

The conference also had a strong commitment to developing the next generation of scientists. More than one-third of attendees were graduate students, postdoctoral fellows, and early-career investigators. A record 68 scientific abstracts were presented, with awards recognizing outstanding trainee research. More than 100 participants took part in structured mentoring activities that paired trainees with established investigators and industry leaders, while dedicated career development sessions provided practical guidance on scientific careers, leadership, and professional development.

The meeting expanded access to advanced research methods through a hands-on workshop where participants received training in state-of-the-art laboratory techniques used to study lung disease and regenerative therapies. These educational activities help ensure that new technologies are disseminated broadly across the research community, accelerating scientific progress.

The conference also strengthened connections between science and the public. An expanded outreach program introduced 28 Vermont high school students to biomedical research through interactive educational activities, inspiring future careers in science, technology, engineering, and medicine (STEM). By engaging students early, the conference helped build the future workforce needed to address major health challenges.

The scientific impact of the conference will continue beyond the meeting through peer-reviewed publications in leading journals, including Cytotherapy, the American Journal of Physiology-Lung Cellular and Molecular Physiology, and a special issue of the American Journal of Respiratory Cell and Molecular Biology. These publications will ensure that the knowledge shared during the conference reaches researchers, clinicians, and educators worldwide.

Overall, the conference advanced scientific understanding of lung regeneration and disease, strengthened international collaborations, trained the next generation of researchers, expanded public engagement in science, and accelerated progress toward developing new regenerative therapies that have the potential to improve the lives of millions of people affected by lung diseases.
